newsitem.title: UK: Vodafone brand comes into the high street.
newsitem.headline: Vodafone brand comes into the high street.

text.p: Vodafone Group Plc, Britain's biggest mobile phone company, is bringing its own name to the high street in an attempt to cut costs, boost brand awareness and capture hesitant new customers.

As part of a new corporate identity unveiled on Monday, the group said a simpler structure and single brand would cost it 300 jobs over the next 18 months and 20 million pounds ($33.8 million) in profits this year.
But it is also expected to stimulate sluggish market growth, strengthen Vodafone's market leadership and help it win 500,000 net new customers per year over the next three years.
The facelift is likely to boost operating profits by 10 million pounds in the second year and 35 million pounds in year three, Vodafone added.
With a confusing number of outlets that sell its telephones, Vodafone has been considered a network operator rather than a retailer.

Six service providers hook customers up to its network and sell its phones in around 270 high street stores using five different billing systems, six customer care systems, 12 brands -- including six retail facias -- and 87 different tariffs.

Armed with an updated logo featuring open speech marks, the company will merge its six service providers into three divisions, each concentrating on a separate market sector -- corporate customers, small businesses and residential customers.
The new businesses, called Vodafone Retail, Vodafone Connect and Vodafone Corporate, will be set up over the next 18 months with one billing and computer system.

The single brand name will cost 15 million pounds to paint on shops, literature and vehicles. Thirty-five million pounds has been set aside in sponsorships and advertising to promote the Vodafone name. The number of different tariffs will also be reduced to 12-20.

The group also plans to close the doors of its high street stores to the telephones of its three rivals -- Orange Plc, Cellnet, majority-owned by British Telecommunications, and One2One, jointly-owned by Cable and Wireless Plc and U S West Inc.
"All our retail outlets will sell and advertise Vodafone and Vodafone only," chief executive Chris Gent told a news conference.
Talkland, Peoples Phone and Astec are currently selling mobile telephones from all four operators but would no longer do so "as of tomorrow", Gent said.

The restructuring comes has been prompted by fiercer competition which ensures fewer differences between operators and makes distribution and after sales service crucial as companies vie for the lower-usage, lower margin and less loyal consumer market.
Vodafone's shares slipped 6.5p to 299.5p on profit-taking in a weaker market. But most analysts welcomed the move to re-brand under one name.
"The fewer names you're spending money on, the better," noted James Golob, telecoms analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Cellular penetration is currently stuck around 13 percent in Britain, compared with five percent in France, 7.5 percent in Germany and the Netherlands and a hefty 29 percent in Sweden.

Although Vodafone expects Scandinavian levels of penetration of 35 percent to come in Britain in 10-12 years, Oliver Ehrenberg, telecoms analyst at Robert Fleming, believes prices have to fall by 15-20 percent to propel penetration to even 20 percent.

Pressure to cut tariffs further has been mounting as Orange, Britain's youngest mobile operator, has rolled out its network and One2One, the smallest cellular company, will also soon have a national network.

Despite recent moves to cut prices -- which have left tariffs at the bottom end of the market almost a third lower than in April -- they remain more than 30 percent higher than in the high penetration high growth countries in Europe, according to Salomon Brothers.
Gent said any price cuts this year are likely to focus on the business sector, but added that Vodafone may cut residential prices next year to entice new customers onto mobile telephones.
